subproblems.title: Integrals over finite sets with respect to H⁰ = μHE[0]
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let F be a finite subset of ℝ^P (a Finset), let f : ℝ^P → ℝ be any function and g : ℝ^P → [0, ∞] any function (no measurability is assumed). Then the Bochner integral of f over F with respect to Mathlib's normalized 0-dimensional Hausdorff measure H⁰ = μHE[0] equals Σ_{x∈F} f(x). Likewise the lower Lebesgue integral of g over F with respect to μHE[0] equals Σ_{x∈F} g(x).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (F : Finset (Euclid P)) (f : Euclid P → ℝ) (g : Euclid P → ℝ≥0∞), (∫ x in (F : Set (Euclid P)), f x ∂μHE[0]) = ∑ x ∈ F, f x ∧ (∫⁻ x in (F : Set (Euclid P)), g x ∂μHE[0]) = ∑ x ∈ F, g x
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof step 1 (H⁰ = μHE[0] = μH[0] is the counting measure, μH[0]{x} = 1) and the finite-set integrals used in parent steps 1 and 6. Simon's printed proof of Ch. 6, 8.2 (book/chapter-06.txt lines 2322–2323) only says that "the theorem is trivial in case n = 0", so this argument is extracted and specialized from the parent-supplied proof (Part III, CL(0)).

1. Normalisation. Mathlib MeasureTheory.Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_zero gives μHE[0] = μH[0] on ℝ^P; rewrite both goals with it. Mathlib MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure_zero_singleton gives μH[0]{x} = 1 for every x ∈ ℝ^P. Singletons of ℝ^P are Borel, hence measurable (MeasurableSingletonClass). So it suffices to prove both identities for μ := μH[0].
2. Integrability of f on F. As sets, F = ⋃_{x∈F} {x} (Set.biUnion_of_singleton). For each x ∈ F, f is integrable on {x} with respect to μ by Mathlib integrableOn_singleton, because ‖f(x)‖ₑ < ∞ (f(x) is a real number) and μ{x} = 1 < ∞. No measurability of f is needed: on {x} the restricted measure is μ{x}·δ_x, and f agrees a.e. with the constant f(x). Integrability on each piece of a finite union gives integrability on the union (Mathlib integrableOn_finite_biUnion, the index set F being finite). Hence f is integrable on F.
3. Bochner integral. With the integrability of step 2, Mathlib MeasureTheory.setIntegral_finset gives ∫_F f dμ = Σ_{x∈F} μ.real{x} • f(x). Here μ.real{x} = (μ{x}).toReal = 1 (measureReal_def), so ∫_F f dμ = Σ_{x∈F} f(x). This is the first identity.
4. Lower integral. For a measure with measurable singletons and a finset F, Mathlib MeasureTheory.lintegral_finset gives ∫⁻_F g dμ = Σ_{x∈F} g(x)·μ{x} for every g : ℝ^P → [0, ∞]; no measurability of g is needed. Since μ{x} = 1, this equals Σ_{x∈F} g(x). This is the second identity.
5. Steps 1–4 prove both identities for μHE[0]. ∎

subproblems.title: A finite set has approximate tangent space {0} in dimension 0 at each of its points
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let F ⊆ ℝ^P be a finite set and let y ∈ F. Then HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 0 F y ⊥ holds (Simon Ch. 3, 1.4 with n = 0). Explicitly: the zero subspace ⊥ = {0} has dimension 0, and for every compactly supported continuous f : ℝ^P → ℝ, ∫_{η_{y,ρ}(F)} f dH⁰ → ∫_{{0}} f dH⁰ = f(0) as ρ → 0 with ρ > 0. Here η_{y,ρ}(z) = ρ⁻¹(z − y) is SimonGMT blowUpMap y ρ and H⁰ = μHE[0].
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (F : Set (Euclid P)) (y : Euclid P), F.Finite → y ∈ F → HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 0 F y ⊥
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof step 6, orientation at y ∈ F: with δ := dist(y, F ∖ {y}) > 0 and f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P) with tsupport f ⊆ B_{R_f}(0), for 0 < ρ < δ/R_f the blow-up ρ⁻¹(F − y) meets tsupport f at most in 0, so HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 0 F y {0}. Simon's printed proof of Ch. 6, 8.2 (book/chapter-06.txt lines 2322–2323) only says that "the theorem is trivial in case n = 0", so this argument is extracted and specialized from the parent-supplied proof (Part III, CL(0)).

Definition used. HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 0 F y Q (SimonGMT Chapter03; Simon Ch. 3, 1.4) means: finrank Q = 0, and for every f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P, ℝ) the function ρ ↦ ∫_{η_{y,ρ}(F)} f dH⁰ tends to ∫_Q f dH⁰ along 𝓝[>] 0, where η_{y,ρ}(z) = ρ⁻¹•(z − y) is SimonGMT blowUpMap y ρ and H⁰ = μHE[0]. We take Q = ⊥ = {0}.

1. Dimension. finrank ℝ (⊥ : Submodule ℝ ℝ^P) = 0 (Mathlib finrank_bot). Fix f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P, ℝ).
2. Limit value. The carrier of ⊥ is {0} (Submodule.bot_coe), the coercion of the finset {0}. The first identity of the sibling theorem cbrz_finset_integral_hausdorff_zero, applied to the finset {0}, gives ∫_⊥ f dH⁰ = f(0).
3. Support radius. tsupport f is compact (f.hasCompactSupport), hence bounded, so tsupport f ⊆ B̄_R(0) for some R ∈ ℝ (Bornology.IsBounded.subset_closedBall). Put R₀ := max(R, 0) + 1 > 0. If ‖z‖ ≥ R₀, then ‖z‖ > R, so z ∉ tsupport f and f(z) = 0 (image_eq_zero_of_notMem_tsupport).
4. Separation radius. F ∖ {y} is finite, hence closed, and does not contain y. Its complement is therefore an open neighbourhood of y, so there is δ > 0 with B_δ(y) ∩ (F ∖ {y}) = ∅ (Metric.isOpen_iff). Thus ‖z − y‖ ≥ δ for every z ∈ F with z ≠ y (vacuous if F = {y}).

1. Cancellation. For p ∈ ℝ^P let m(p) := Σ_{l<M} (if y_l = p then v_l else 0) ∈ ℤ. Let Y := {y_l : l < M} (the finset image of range M under y) and G := {p ∈ Y : p ∈ V and m(p) ≠ 0} (Finset.filter), a finite subset of V.

subproblems.title: Limits of bounded weighted point sums in a compact set are finite integer point sums
subproblems.statement: Let P, C ∈ ℕ and let K ⊆ ℝ^P be compact. Let N : ℕ → ℕ, w : ℕ → ℕ → ℤ and x : ℕ → ℕ → ℝ^P satisfy x_{j,l} ∈ K and w_{j,l} ≠ 0 whenever l < N_j, and Σ_{l<N_j} |w_{j,l}| ≤ C for every j. Let ι be a type, and for k ∈ ι let g_k : ℝ^P → ℝ be continuous and t_k ∈ ℝ, such that Σ_{l<N_j} w_{j,l} g_k(x_{j,l}) → t_k as j → ∞ for every k. Then there are M ∈ ℕ, v : ℕ → ℤ and y : ℕ → ℝ^P with y_l ∈ K for l < M and t_k = Σ_{l<M} v_l g_k(y_l) for every k ∈ ι.

Source: parent proof steps 4–5: N_j and the signs take finitely many values and B̄_{2r}(x₀)^N is compact, so a subsequence has constant count, constant signs and convergent points, and the limit is identified by continuity. Here integer weights w_{j,l} replace points listed |w_{j,l}| times with sign ±1; the bounds of step 1 give the same finiteness. Simon's printed proof of Ch. 6, 8.2 (book/chapter-06.txt lines 2322–2323) only says that "the theorem is trivial in case n = 0", so this argument is extracted and specialized from the parent-supplied proof (Part III, CL(0)).

1. Bounds. For l < N_j, w_{j,l} ≠ 0 gives |w_{j,l}| ≥ 1 (Int.natAbs_pos), so N_j = Σ_{l<N_j} 1 ≤ Σ_{l<N_j} |w_{j,l}| ≤ C. Also |w_{j,l}| ≤ Σ_{l'<N_j} |w_{j,l'}| ≤ C for l < N_j (Finset.single_le_sum), i.e. −C ≤ w_{j,l} ≤ C.
2. Constant combinatorial type. Put δ_j := (N_j, u_j) ∈ ℕ × ℤ^{Fin C}, where u_j(l) := w_{j,l} if l < N_j and u_j(l) := 0 otherwise (l ranging over Fin C). By step 1, every δ_j lies in the finite set S := {0, …, C} × {−C, …, C}^{Fin C}. Since ℕ is infinite and S is finite, some d = (N₀, u₀) ∈ S has an infinite fibre (Mathlib Finite.exists_infinite_fiber), i.e. δ_j = d frequently along atTop (Nat.frequently_atTop_iff_infinite). Hence there is a strictly increasing φ₁ : ℕ → ℕ with δ_{φ₁(j)} = d for all j (extraction_of_frequently_atTop). Consequently N_{φ₁(j)} = N₀ ≤ C and w_{φ₁(j),l} = u₀(l) for all j and all l < N₀.
3. Convergent points. X_j := (x_{φ₁(j),l})_{l<N₀} ∈ (ℝ^P)^{Fin N₀} lies in K^{Fin N₀} because N_{φ₁(j)} = N₀, and K^{Fin N₀} is compact (Mathlib isCompact_univ_pi). As (ℝ^P)^{Fin N₀} is a metric space, there are a ∈ K^{Fin N₀} and a strictly increasing φ₂ with X_{φ₂(j)} → a (Mathlib IsCompact.tendsto_subseq). Put ψ := φ₁ ∘ φ₂; it is strictly increasing, so ψ(j) → ∞ (StrictMono.tendsto_atTop).
4. Identification of the limit. Fix k ∈ ι. By step 2 and reindexing (Finset.sum_range), for every j,
Σ_{l<N_{ψ(j)}} w_{ψ(j),l} g_k(x_{ψ(j),l}) = Σ_{l<N₀} u₀(l) g_k(X_{φ₂(j)}(l)).
(i) The left side tends to t_k: it is the hypothesis' convergent sequence composed with ψ → ∞ (Tendsto.comp).
(ii) The right side tends to Σ_{l<N₀} u₀(l) g_k(a_l): each coordinate X_{φ₂(j)}(l) → a_l (continuity of evaluation, continuous_apply), g_k is continuous, and finite sums and constant multiples of convergent sequences converge (tendsto_finsetSum, Tendsto.const_mul).
By uniqueness of limits in ℝ (tendsto_nhds_unique), t_k = Σ_{l<N₀} u₀(l) g_k(a_l).
5. Put M := N₀; v_l := u₀(l) for l < C and v_l := 0 for l ≥ C (so v_l = u₀(l) for l < N₀ ≤ C); y_l := a_l for l < N₀ and y_l := 0 for l ≥ N₀. Then y_l ∈ K for l < M because a ∈ K^{Fin N₀}, and by step 4 (and Finset.sum_range) t_k = Σ_{l<M} v_l g_k(y_l) for every k ∈ ι. ∎
